Saudi Arabia Industrial Output Slumps 23.5% in August
body: Industrial production in Saudi Arabia slumped 23.5% year-on-year in August 2026, deepening from an upwardly revised 8.3% decline in July. The oil sector contracted sharply by 33.66%, compared with an 11.4% fall in the previous month, driven by steeper drops in both crude petroleum and natural gas extraction (-35.8% vs. -10.9%) and the production of coke and refined petroleum products (-24.1% vs. -13.6%). This substantial decline was partly cushioned by stronger growth in other economic activities, whose output expanded 5.1% (up from 3.4%). Within this segment, electricity, gas, steam, and air-conditioning supply accelerated markedly (9.4% vs. 4.5%), while water supply, sewerage, waste management, and remediation activities grew at a slightly slower pace (7.4% vs. 7.8%). The downturn was also mitigated by a return to growth in non-oil activities, which rose 1.2% year-on-year after a 0.3% decline in July, although manufacturing output edged down by 0.3%. On a monthly basis, total industrial production dropped 14.0% in August, swinging from a downwardly revised 10.0% increase recorded in July. body: Egypt's core consumer price inflation slowed to 14.10% year-on-year in September 2026, down from 14.90% in August 2026, according to data updated on 11 October 2026. The reading, measured on a year-over-year basis, reflects the change in prices this September compared with September a year earlier, while the previous figure captured the annual change for August. The latest data indicate a continued easing in underlying price pressures, with core CPI decelerating for the second consecutive month. Core inflation excludes the most volatile components of the consumer basket, making it a closely watched gauge of persistent inflation trends. Investors and policymakers will be assessing whether this moderation in core prices signals a more durable shift in Egypt's inflation dynamics or a temporary relief in a still-elevated price environment. title: Weekend: Musk says $15 billion Terrafab can make chips better than anyone, given time
body: For chip stocks, the remarks reinforce that Terrafab is a long-dated threat to incumbent foundries rather than a near-term one, which limits any read-across to TSMC and Samsung while Musk's companies keep buying their output. Intel stands to gain the most direct benefit as a joint venture partner, giving its foundry ambitions a high-profile anchor customer. For Tesla, the project adds a large, open-ended capital commitment with a multi-year payoff, a factor investors will weigh against the strategic value of securing AI chip supply. Musk's admission on timing may help temper expectations that had run ahead of execution. --- Earlier: Why a few words from Elon Musk can (and did!) move a $600 billion+ chipmaker SpaceX just officially announced two massive milestones for Starlink Mobile --- Musk still thinks he can beat the world's chipmakers at their own game, but for once he isn't promising to do it quickly.

title: More on Russia's diesel U-turn: 500,000 tons cleared for export after Trump-Putin deal
body: For oil product, the immediate volume is modest: around 500,000 tons equals roughly 3.7 million barrels, small against global diesel trade, so the price effect rests more on what follows than on this tranche. The signal matters more for middle distillate margins, as a Russian return to export markets, alongside a pause in Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, would ease one of the tighter corners of the fuel market. Buyers may move cautiously, since US sanctions passed last month still target Russian energy revenues and contract terms remain unclear. Any confirmation of further tranches would add downside pressure to diesel cracks in Europe and Asia. --- Moscow has turned on the diesel tap, but only partway, and on its own schedule rather than the one Trump announced.

title: Monday: Thin start for Asia as Tokyo shuts for Sports Day and US Treasuries stay closed. A huge week follows.
body: Monday's closures in Tokyo and the US cash Treasury market mean thinner liquidity across Asia and into the US session, which can exaggerate moves on weekend headlines from Saudi Arabia, Russia and Ukraine. Singapore, Hong Kong, Australia and New Zealand are all open though For oil, the week links directly to inflation: energy has been the main force holding US headline CPI above 3%, so any renewed crude strength from Gulf attacks would feed expectations of further Fed tightening, while the Russian diesel deal and energy ceasefire point the other way for fuel prices. A hot CPI print would likely lift the front end of the Treasury curve and support the dollar, putting pressure on the yen. Bank results offer an early read on credit quality under higher rates. --- A quiet Monday in Tokyo and on the Treasury desk gives way to the week's real business: inflation, the banks and one last hearing from Warsh.

title: Trump says Russia, Ukraine agree energy ceasefire two days after Russian diesel deal
body: For oil, the two announcements point the same way for diesel: more Russian supply. The deal adds Russian barrels directly, while a halt to Ukrainian strikes on Russian fuel infrastructure would remove a recurring threat to the country's refining and export capacity, a combination that would weigh on diesel margins if it holds. Traders are likely to discount both until details emerge, as the Kremlin has not publicly confirmed the truce terms and the delivery schedule rests on Trump's own description. The broader signal is a weaker US commitment to squeezing Russian energy revenues, which erodes part of the sanctions-related risk premium in crude. --- Earlier: Houthi strike on Riyadh airport kills 13, group claims Aramco hits. Saudi, Iran talking now. Delivered crude prices surge back to highs as JPMorgan flags tanker crunch --- In the space of a weekend, Washington went from sanctioning Russian energy to buying it, then declared a truce over it.

title: Houthi strike on Riyadh airport kills 13, group claims Aramco hits. Saudi, Iran talking now.
body: For oil, the shift in targeting matters more than the airport damage: claimed strikes on two Aramco facilities and a confirmed hit on Dammam bring the conflict into the Eastern Province, the centre of Saudi crude output. With Aramco silent, traders are left to price the risk without knowing whether any production or export capacity was affected, which tends to support a geopolitical premium until damage is clarified. The timing adds pressure, as JPMorgan noted last week that the global tanker fleet is already close to full use, so any disruption to Gulf loadings or routing would land on a market with little shipping slack. The Saudi-Iranian contact is the main counterweight, and any sign of de-escalation could quickly erode that premium. --- The Houthis are no longer just hitting Riyadh's runways; they say they are now aiming at the kingdom's oil, and Riyadh has picked up the phone to Tehran.

title: Delivered crude prices surge back to highs as JPMorgan flags tanker crunch
body: For oil, the note describes a market where the cost of delivery, rather than the barrel itself, is setting the marginal price. That can widen the gap between benchmark futures and what refiners actually pay, and it tends to reward freight exposure more directly than outright crude. Negative European refining margins raise the risk of run cuts, which would trim crude demand and could cap benchmark prices even while delivered costs stay high. Atlantic Basin grades moved on smaller ships carry higher per-barrel freight, a possible headwind for their competitiveness in distant markets. --- Where we left off Friday: investingLive Americas FX news wrap 9 Oct: It's a Wrap: Stocks rebound despite weak sentiment; Canadian dollar falls on jobs miss --- The oil market has found its April again, only this time the scarce commodity is the ship, not the crude.
